questions.s: Concerning the sphenoid and palatine bones (Last's):
o: The lateral pterygoid plate attaches at the anterior pole of foramen ovale

The lateral pterygoid plate is attached to the skull base at the anterior edge (pole) of foramen ovale.
It is the landmark for a mandibular nerve block: the needle passes behind it to reach V3. (Last's p. 653)
The pyramidal process of the palatine bone fills the pterygoid notch

The pyramidal process of the palatine bone fills the notch between the lower ends of the medial and lateral pterygoid plates.
It locks the palatine bone to the sphenoid. (Last's p. 653)
The lateral pterygoid plate extends back and medially into the nasopharynx

The lateral pterygoid plate extends back and laterally into the infratemporal fossa, giving origin to both pterygoid muscles.
The medial plate faces the nasopharynx. (Last's p. 653)
The perpendicular plate of the palatine bone forms the lateral wall of the pterygopalatine fossa

The perpendicular plate of the palatine bone, with the medial pterygoid plate, forms the medial wall of the pterygopalatine fossa.
The sphenopalatine foramen is in this medial wall. (Last's p. 653)
The anterior margin of the prechiasmatic groove divides anterior from middle fossae centrally

Centrally, the anterior margin of the prechiasmatic groove marks the boundary between the anterior and middle cranial fossae. So the optic canals lie in the middle fossa.
Laterally the boundary is the posterior edge of the lesser wings. (Last's p. 653)
The jugum joins the two lesser wings

The jugum of the sphenoid joins the two lesser wings and articulates in front with the cribriform plate.
It forms the central part of the anterior fossa floor. (Last's p. 653)
The squamous part of the frontal bone is the largest contributor to its floor

The orbital part of the frontal bone is the largest contributor to the floor of the anterior cranial fossa.
The squamous part forms the forehead and the front wall. (Last's p. 653)
The foramen caecum lies in front of the crista galli and above the frontal crest

The foramen caecum lies behind the lower end of the frontal crest, in front of the crista galli.
It is usually a blind pit plugged by the falx. (Last's p. 653)
A dural flange between middle and posterior clinoids separates cavernous sinus from pituitary fossa

A dural flange running between the middle and posterior clinoid processes hangs vertically and separates the cavernous sinus from the pituitary fossa.
It forms the medial wall of the sinus. (Last's p. 653)
The anterior clinoid tip carries the ridge continuing as the free tentorial edge

A ridge of dura from the tip of the anterior clinoid process runs back along the lateral roof of the cavernous sinus and continues as the free edge of the tentorium.
III and IV pierce the roof medial to this ridge. (Last's p. 653)
The free edge ridge passes medial to the posterior clinoid process

The ridge continuing as the free edge passes lateral to the posterior clinoid process.
The attached margin of the tentorium ends at the posterior clinoid process. (Last's p. 653)
The spheno-occipital synchondrosis ossifies at about 15 years

Last's says the spheno-occipital synchondrosis ossifies at about the twenty-fifth year, not at 15.
It is a growth site for the cranial base. (Last's p. 653)
The floors of the middle and posterior fossae ossify in cartilage

The floors of the middle and posterior cranial fossae (the skull base) are preformed in cartilage and ossify in cartilage.
The chondrocranium. (Last's p. 653)
The vault and face ossify in membrane

The vault and the facial bones ossify directly in membrane.
The mandible ossifies mainly in membrane too. (Last's p. 653)
The lacrimal bone completes the ethmoid labyrinth posteriorly

The lacrimal bone completes the ethmoid labyrinth anteriorly. Posteriorly it is completed by the sphenoidal concha and the orbital process of the palatine.
The labyrinth is open in the isolated ethmoid. (Last's p. 653)
The roof of the ethmoid labyrinth is the cribriform plate

The roof of the ethmoid labyrinth is formed by the orbital part of the frontal bone, not the cribriform plate.
The cribriform plate lies medial to the labyrinth, at a lower level. (Last's p. 653)
The infundibulum leads from the frontal sinus to the middle meatus

The ethmoidal infundibulum leads from the frontal sinus, through the frontonasal duct, to the middle meatus.
It opens into the hiatus semilunaris. (Last's p. 653)
The superior and middle conchae arise from a common stem

The superior and middle conchae arise from a common stem on the ethmoid labyrinth and diverge posteriorly.
The superior meatus lies between them. (Last's p. 653)
The superior concha is the larger of the two ethmoidal conchae

The middle concha is larger than the superior concha.
The inferior concha is a separate bone. (Last's p. 653)
The middle concha articulates posteriorly with the perpendicular plate of the palatine just above the sphenopalatine foramen

The middle concha articulates posteriorly with the perpendicular plate of the palatine just below the sphenopalatine foramen.
The foramen therefore lies above its posterior end. (Last's p. 653)
Nothing intervenes between pia and the underlying nervous tissue

Nothing intervenes between the pia and the underlying nervous tissue. The pia lies directly on the brain and cord and follows every sulcus.
It is the innermost of the meninges. (Last's p. 559)
It fuses with the epineurium of cranial and spinal nerves

The pia continues over the cranial nerves and spinal roots and fuses with their epineurium.
So the subarachnoid space ends where the pia meets the nerve sheath. (Last's p. 559)
It is avascular

The pia is vascular, containing blood vessels, like periosteum.
The vessels pass through it into the brain. (Last's p. 559)
Cerebral arteries are tightly adherent to their pial sheaths

Cerebral arteries lie loose in pial sheaths in a space containing CSF.
This perivascular space allows movement. (Last's p. 559)

questions.s: The arachnoid mater and subdural space (Last's):
o: The subdural space contains only a thin film of tissue fluid

The arachnoid is supported by the dura with only a film of tissue fluid between them; the subdural space is a potential space.
Blood can open it up to form a subdural haematoma. (Last's p. 559)
Dura and arachnoid blend at the aqueduct of the cochlea

The dura and arachnoid blend at the aqueduct of the cochlea, the sole exception to their separateness.
Here the perilymph communicates with the subarachnoid space. (Last's p. 559)
Vessels run along between dura and arachnoid

Vessels pierce the dura and arachnoid at the same place and never run between them.
Bridging veins cross the subdural space where they pierce both layers together. (Last's p. 559)
Dura and arachnoid become continuous with each other like the pleurae

Unlike the visceral and parietal pleurae, the dura and arachnoid never become continuous with each other.
They remain separate layers throughout. (Last's p. 559)
They are most numerous in the superior sagittal sinus and its lakes

Arachnoid villi are most numerous in the superior sagittal sinus and its lateral lakes. With age they clump into granulations.
They are the main route for CSF absorption. (Last's p. 559)
In children they are discrete

In children the arachnoid villi are discrete. With age they aggregate into Pacchionian bodies (granulations).
These may erode the inner table of the skull. (Last's p. 559)
The spinal subarachnoid space ends at L2

The spinal subarachnoid space ends at the level of S2, not L2.
L2 is roughly the end of the spinal cord. (Last's p. 559)
The spinal web-like strands form a complete anterior septum

In the spinal canal the web-like arachnoid strands form an incomplete posterior median septum, not a complete anterior septum.
Anteriorly there is no septum. (Last's p. 559)
The cisterna magna is the largest cistern

The cerebellomedullary cistern (cisterna magna), between the cerebellum and medulla, is the largest cistern.
It can be punctured through the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane. (Last's p. 559)
The cisterna magna contains the vertebral artery and PICA laterally

Laterally the cisterna magna contains the vertebral artery and PICA on each side.
The median aperture of the fourth ventricle opens into it. (Last's p. 559)
The pontine cistern receives CSF from the median aperture

The pontine cistern receives CSF from the lateral apertures. The median aperture opens into the cisterna magna.
Median = magna; lateral = pontine. (Last's p. 559)
The pontine cistern contains the third and fourth cranial nerves

The pontine cistern contains the fifth to twelfth cranial nerves and the basilar artery. III and IV are in the interpeduncular cistern.
So the pontine cistern is a busy place for cranial nerves. (Last's p. 559)
The interpeduncular cistern lies between dorsum sellae and cerebral peduncles

The interpeduncular cistern lies between the dorsum sellae and the cerebral peduncles, roofed by the floor of the third ventricle.
It is the site of endoscopic third ventriculostomy. (Last's p. 559)
It contains the pituitary stalk

It contains the pituitary stalk, the top of the basilar artery and the posterior part of the circle of Willis, and III and IV.
Aneurysms of the basilar tip lie here. (Last's p. 559)
The chiasmatic cistern lies below the optic chiasma

The chiasmatic cistern lies above the optic chiasma, beneath the rostrum of the corpus callosum.
It extends in front of the lamina terminalis. (Last's p. 559)
The anterior communicating artery lies in the interpeduncular cistern

The anterior communicating artery lies in the chiasmatic cistern.
The interpeduncular cistern holds the posterior part of the circle. (Last's p. 559)

questions.s: The outer layer of the dura (Last's):
o: It is periosteum

The outer layer of the cranial dura is simply the periosteum (endosteum) of the skull bones.
That is why it adheres to the bone. (Last's p. 560)
It is continuous with pericranium around every foramen

At each foramen the outer layer is continuous with the pericranium on the outside of the skull.
So it is part of the skull's periosteal covering. (Last's p. 560)
It continues into the spinal dura

The outer (periosteal) layer is not prolonged into the vertebral canal. The spinal dura is the continuation of the inner (meningeal) layer.
The spinal extradural space lies between the dura and the vertebral periosteum. (Last's p. 560)
It is invaginated by cranial nerves

The outer layer is never invaginated by any cranial nerve. Nerves carry sleeves of the inner layer.
The outer layer just passes out through the foramina as pericranium. (Last's p. 560)
Over the vault it strips easily from bone

Over the vault the dura strips easily from the bone. Over the base it strips only with difficulty.
So extradural haematomas form mainly over the vault. (Last's p. 560)
Middle meningeal vessels are usually described as extradural

The middle meningeal vessels bulge from the outer surface of the dura and groove the bone, so bleeding from them is extradural.
This is the classic extradural haematoma after a temporal fracture. (Last's p. 560)
The venous sinuses lie outside the outer layer

The venous sinuses lie between the two layers of dura, not outside the outer layer.
They are endothelium-lined channels within the dura. (Last's p. 560)
The inner layer leaves the outer at the jugular foramen to form spinal dura

The inner layer leaves the outer at the foramen magnum to form the spinal dura.
The jugular foramen transmits the internal jugular vein and IX, X, XI. (Last's p. 560)
Its attached margin carries the transverse and superior petrosal sinuses

The attached margin of the tentorium encloses the transverse sinuses behind and the superior petrosal sinuses along the petrous ridge.
These are its two sinus-bearing parts. (Last's p. 560)
Its free margin contains no venous sinus

The free margin of the tentorium, around the tentorial notch, contains no venous sinus.
The midbrain passes through the notch. (Last's p. 560)
Its free margin lies lower than its bony attachment

The free margin lies at a higher level than the bony attachment; the tentorium rises to a ridge in the middle.
That is why it is tent-shaped. (Last's p. 560)
The straight sinus slopes at less than 30 degrees in the intact dura

Last's says the straight sinus slopes down more steeply than 45 degrees in the intact dura.
The angle reflects the tent shape. (Last's p. 560)

questions.s: Regarding the free margin of the tentorium:
o: It is traceable forwards to the anterior clinoid process

The free margin of the tentorium runs forward past the posterior clinoid to the anterior clinoid process.
It forms the boundary of the tentorial notch. (Last's p. 560)
The roof medial to it is pierced by III and IV

III and IV pierce the roof of the cavernous sinus medial to the ridge continued from the free margin.
That is why uncal herniation over the edge compresses III. (Last's p. 560)
It is attached to the posterior clinoid processes

The attached margin is fixed to the posterior clinoid processes. The free margin reaches the anterior clinoid processes.
The two margins cross each other. (Last's p. 560)
It falls down if the tentorium is divided

Last's says the tentorium falls if the falx is divided, because the falx holds it up.
Dividing the tentorium does not make it fall. (Last's p. 560)
Its anterior end projects into the foramen caecum like an enlarged Sharpey's fibre

The anterior end of the falx plugs the foramen caecum like an enlarged Sharpey's fibre.
Only rarely does the foramen transmit a vein. (Last's p. 561)
Its free lower border contains the inferior sagittal sinus

The free lower border of the falx contains the inferior sagittal sinus, lying just above the corpus callosum.
It joins the great cerebral vein to form the straight sinus. (Last's p. 561)
The superior sagittal sinus begins at the crista galli

The superior sagittal sinus begins a short distance above the foramen caecum, not at the crista galli.
It runs back in the attached upper border of the falx. (Last's p. 561)
The superior sagittal sinus narrows as it passes back

The superior sagittal sinus becomes progressively broader as it passes back, receiving more veins.
It is widest near the confluence. (Last's p. 561)

questions.s: The falx cerebelli and diaphragma sellae (Last's):
o: The falx cerebelli lodges the occipital sinus

The falx cerebelli is a low midline fold along the internal occipital crest, containing the occipital sinus.
It projects between the cerebellar hemispheres. (Last's p. 561)
The diaphragma sellae is perforated for the pituitary stalk

The diaphragma sellae roofs the pituitary fossa and has a central opening for the pituitary stalk.
The size of the opening varies. (Last's p. 561)
The falx cerebelli extends to the anterior margin of the foramen magnum

The falx cerebelli extends down to the posterior margin of the foramen magnum.
The occipital sinus may run around the foramen to the sigmoid sinuses. (Last's p. 561)
The diaphragma sellae is formed from the outer dural layer

The diaphragma sellae, like the other dural folds, is formed from the inner (meningeal) layer of dura.
The outer layer stays on the bone. (Last's p. 561)
The accessory meningeal artery enters through foramen ovale

The accessory meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, enters the skull through foramen ovale.
It supplies dura over the cavernous sinus and the trigeminal ganglion. (Last's p. 562)
Posterior fossa dura receives meningeal branches of the vertebral

The dura of the posterior cranial fossa receives meningeal branches of the vertebral artery, entering at the foramen magnum.
Meningeal branches of the occipital and ascending pharyngeal arteries also contribute. (Last's p. 562)
The inner dural layer has a rich blood supply

Last's says the inner layer of the dura needs very little blood. The outer (periosteal) layer is richly supplied, mainly to nourish the bone.
The meningeal arteries are really periosteal arteries. (Last's p. 562)
The accessory meningeal artery supplies the anterior cranial fossa

The accessory meningeal artery supplies the dura over the cavernous sinus (and the trigeminal ganglion), not the anterior cranial fossa.
The anterior fossa is supplied by ethmoidal branches of the ophthalmic artery. (Last's p. 562)
Passes between the two roots of the auriculotemporal nerve

The middle meningeal artery runs up between the two roots of the auriculotemporal nerve to reach foramen spinosum.
This relation helps identify the artery below the skull. (Last's p. 562)
Its veins lie between it and the bone

The middle meningeal veins lie between the artery and the bone, and it is the veins that are responsible for the grooves in the skull.
So a fracture may tear the veins as well as the artery. (Last's p. 562)
Its anterior branch lies over the postcentral gyrus

The anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery lies over the precentral gyrus, so haemorrhage presses on the motor area and causes contralateral weakness.
The postcentral gyrus is just behind. (Last's p. 562)
Its posterior branch haemorrhage may cause ipsilateral deafness

Haemorrhage from the posterior branch may cause contralateral deafness, by pressure on the auditory area.
Each auditory cortex receives mainly from the opposite ear (though representation is bilateral). (Last's p. 562)
Near the pterion it often lies in a bony tunnel for a centimetre or more

Near the pterion the anterior branch often runs in a bony tunnel for a centimetre or more, so it is easily torn by fractures here.
This is the classic source of an extradural haematoma. (Last's p. 562)
Its main purpose is to supply the vault bones

The main purpose of the middle meningeal artery is to supply the bones of the vault. It does not supply the brain.
So "meningeal" artery is something of a misnomer. (Last's p. 562)
Scalping causes necrosis of the underlying bone

Very little blood reaches the skull bones from the scalp vessels, so scalping does not cause necrosis of the underlying bone.
The bone is supplied from the dural side. (Last's p. 562)
There are two frontal diploic veins on each side

Last's describes one frontal, two parietal (anterior and posterior temporal) and one occipital diploic vein on each side.
So there is one frontal diploic vein, not two. (Last's p. 562)
The pterion lies 3 cm above the midpoint of the zygomatic arch

The pterion lies about 3 cm above the midpoint of the zygomatic arch, behind the frontozygomatic suture. This is Last's burr-hole site for the anterior branch.
Many other texts give 4 cm. (Last's p. 562)
Foramen spinosum lies just above the articular eminence

Foramen spinosum lies at a level just above the articular eminence at the posterior root of the zygomatic arch.
The artery enters the skull here. (Last's p. 562)
Most middle meningeal veins drain to the pterygoid plexus

Most middle meningeal veins join the sphenoparietal sinus.
Some drain to the pterygoid plexus through foramen spinosum or ovale. (Last's p. 562)
The posterior branch is exposed above the mastoid at the level of the lower orbital margin

The posterior branch is exposed above the mastoid at the level of the upper margin of the orbit.
A horizontal line from the upper orbital margin is the guide. (Last's p. 562)
The tentorial nerves supply the falx and upper surface of the tentorium

Tentorial branches of V1 supply the falx, the dura of the vault and the upper surface of the tentorium.
Supratentorial dural pain is therefore felt in V1 territory. (Last's p. 562)
The posterior fossa is supplied by IX and X

Meningeal branches of IX and X supply the dura of the posterior cranial fossa, with C1 to C3 around the foramen magnum.
Posterior fossa pain refers to the occiput and neck. (Last's p. 562)
The under surface of the tentorium is supplied by the tentorial nerves

The under surface of the tentorium is supplied by IX and X (and upper cervical nerves), not by the tentorial branches of V1.
V1 supplies only the upper surface. (Last's p. 562)
Dura around the foramen magnum is supplied by C4 to C6

The dura around the foramen magnum is supplied by the upper three cervical nerves.
C4 to C6 have no meningeal supply here. (Last's p. 562)
The inferior sagittal and straight sinuses do not lie between the two dural layers

The inferior sagittal and straight sinuses lie within folds of the inner layer of dura (the falx and tentorium), not between the two layers.
The other sinuses lie between the periosteal and meningeal layers. (Last's p. 563-4)
They contain no valves

The venous sinuses are endothelium-lined channels held open by rigid dura, and they have no valves.
Flow can therefore reverse. (Last's p. 563-4)
The superior sagittal sinus drains the frontal pole

The superior sagittal sinus does not drain the frontal pole.
The frontal pole drains to the anterior cerebral and other basal veins. (Last's p. 563-4)
Superior cerebral veins enter with the bloodstream

Superior cerebral veins enter the sinus obliquely against the bloodstream.
This oblique entry may act as a kind of valve. (Last's p. 563-4)
The superior sagittal usually turns to the right

At the internal occipital protuberance the superior sagittal sinus usually turns right into the right transverse sinus.
So the right internal jugular vein is usually larger. (Last's p. 563-4)
The straight sinus usually turns to the left

The straight sinus usually turns left, so deep venous blood drains mainly through the left transverse sinus.
There is often only a small connection between the two at the confluence. (Last's p. 563-4)
The straight sinus receives the superior sagittal sinus

The straight sinus receives the inferior sagittal sinus, the basal veins and the great cerebral vein, not the superior sagittal sinus.
The superior sagittal sinus continues into a transverse sinus. (Last's p. 563-4)
The inferior sagittal sinus begins at the crista galli

The inferior sagittal sinus begins some distance above the crista galli in the free lower border of the falx.
The superior sagittal sinus begins near the foramen caecum. (Last's p. 563-4)
The transverse sinus grooves the mastoid angle of the parietal bone

The transverse sinus grooves the occipital bone and the mastoid angle of the parietal bone before becoming the sigmoid sinus.
It runs in the attached margin of the tentorium. (Last's p. 563-4)
The transverse sinus is marked along the superior nuchal line

The surface marking of the transverse sinus runs along the superior nuchal line from the external occipital protuberance to the top of the mastoid.
The asterion overlies its junction with the sigmoid sinus. (Last's p. 563-4)
The smaller transverse sinus receives the superior sagittal

The larger transverse sinus (usually the right) receives the superior sagittal sinus.
The smaller (usually left) receives the straight sinus. (Last's p. 563-4)
The jugular bulb occupies the anterior compartment of the jugular foramen

The jugular bulb occupies the posterior and largest compartment of the jugular foramen.
The anterior compartment holds the inferior petrosal sinus and IX. (Last's p. 563-4)

questions.s: Connections of the sigmoid and occipital sinuses:
o: The mastoid emissary vein joins the posterior auricular vein

The mastoid emissary vein links the sigmoid sinus with the posterior auricular vein. Infection can spread along it from the scalp or mastoid.
It passes through the mastoid foramen. (Last's p. 563-4)
The occipital sinus drains the choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle

The occipital sinus receives veins from the cerebellum and medulla and drains the choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle.
It lies in the falx cerebelli. (Last's p. 563-4)
The posterior condylar emissary vein joins the pterygoid plexus

The posterior condylar emissary vein joins the suboccipital venous plexus, not the pterygoid plexus.
The pterygoid plexus connects with the cavernous sinus through foramen ovale. (Last's p. 563-4)
Veins accompany the vertebral and basilar arteries intracranially

Last's says no veins accompany the vertebral and basilar arteries intracranially.
The brainstem drains to petrosal and occipital sinuses instead. (Last's p. 563-4)
It receives blood from three sources

The cavernous sinus receives blood from three sources: the orbit (ophthalmic veins), the bones of the vault (middle meningeal veins) and the cerebral hemisphere (superficial middle cerebral vein).
Infection from the face can therefore reach it. (Last's p. 564-6)
It drains by superior and inferior petrosal sinuses and a vein to the pterygoid plexus

The cavernous sinus drains through the superior and inferior petrosal sinuses and an emissary vein to the pterygoid plexus.
The intercavernous sinuses link the two sides. (Last's p. 564-6)
Its capacity is about 15 ml

Last's gives the capacity of the cavernous sinus as about 1.5 ml, not 15 ml.
The factor of ten is the trap. (Last's p. 564-6)
It is free of septa

The cavernous sinus is intersected by numerous fibrous septa, giving it a cavernous (trabeculated) appearance.
That is the origin of its name. (Last's p. 564-6)
III, IV, V1 and V2 lie in the lateral wall

III, IV, V1 and V2 lie in the lateral wall, between the dura and the endothelium. VI and the internal carotid artery lie in the cavity.
So VI is most exposed to intrasinus lesions. (Last's p. 564-6)
The anterior wall plugs the medial end of the superior orbital fissure

The narrow anterior wall plugs the medial end of the superior orbital fissure and receives the ophthalmic veins.
This is the route by which orbital infection reaches the sinus. (Last's p. 564-6)
The lateral wall attaches lateral to foramen ovale

The lateral wall attaches medial to foramen ovale and Meckel's cave.
V3 therefore leaves without entering the sinus. (Last's p. 564-6)
The medial wall is entirely inner dura

The medial wall is formed mostly by the endosteum of the body of the sphenoid, completed by inner dura beside the pituitary fossa.
So it is not entirely inner dura. (Last's p. 564-6)
The trigeminal cave lies posteroinferiorly in the floor of the middle fossa

The trigeminal cave lies behind and below the cavernous sinus, in the floor of the middle fossa.
The ganglion is close to the back of the sinus. (Last's p. 566)
The uncus lies further back and somewhat above the roof

The uncus of the temporal lobe lies further back and somewhat above the roof of the cavernous sinus.
It is close to III and the tentorial edge. (Last's p. 566)
The sphenoidal air sinus lies behind the pituitary fossa at a higher level

The sphenoidal sinus lies towards the front of the pituitary fossa at a lower level, extending further back with age.
It is below, not behind and above. (Last's p. 566)
The cerebral peduncle lies anteriorly

The cerebral peduncle lies posteriorly. The orbital apex lies anteriorly.
The sinus runs from the orbit back to the petrous apex. (Last's p. 566)

questions.s: Lying within the cavity of the cavernous sinus, rather than in its lateral wall, is/are:
o: The oculomotor nerve

III lies in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, not in its cavity.
It is the highest nerve in the wall. (Last's p. 566)
The internal carotid artery

The internal carotid artery runs through the cavity of the sinus, surrounded by venous blood.
A rupture produces a carotid–cavernous fistula. (Last's p. 566)
The maxillary nerve

V2 lies in the lowest part of the lateral wall.
It leaves through foramen rotundum. (Last's p. 566)
The abducent nerve

VI runs in the cavity lateral to the internal carotid artery, not in the wall. That is why it is often affected first by cavernous lesions.
Answer B: 2 and 4. (Last's p. 566)

questions.s: The internal carotid artery in the cavernous sinus (Last's):
o: Enters the posterior part of the sinus from foramen lacerum

The internal carotid artery enters the back of the cavernous sinus after curving up from the foramen lacerum.
It is surrounded by the sympathetic plexus. (Last's p. 566)
Deeply grooves the medial wall of the sinus

The artery arches up and forward in an S-bend that grooves the medial wall of the sinus (the body of the sphenoid).
This is the carotid groove. (Last's p. 566)
Pierces the roof lateral to the anterior clinoid process

The internal carotid pierces the roof of the sinus medial to the anterior clinoid process.
It then gives off the ophthalmic artery. (Last's p. 566)
Carries a sympathetic plexus from the middle cervical ganglion

The sympathetic plexus on the internal carotid comes from the superior cervical ganglion.
Lesions here cause Horner's syndrome. (Last's p. 566)
The abducent runs on the lateral side of the internal carotid

VI runs on the lateral side of the internal carotid artery in the sinus. Further forward it lies below the upturning artery.
It then enters the tendinous ring. (Last's p. 567)
No nerve lies lateral to the trigeminal branches

The trigeminal branches are the most lateral nerves in the cavernous sinus; nothing lies lateral to them.
They are in the lateral wall. (Last's p. 567)
No nerve lies medial to the oculomotor

It is VI that has no nerve medial to it. III lies in the lateral wall.
Last's: no nerve lies medial to VI, and none lateral to the trigeminal branches. (Last's p. 567)
The trochlear enters the superior orbital fissure below and medial to the oculomotor

IV enters the superior orbital fissure at a higher level and lateral to III, passing outside the tendinous ring.
III enters within the ring. (Last's p. 567)

questions.s: The ophthalmic division in the cavernous sinus:
o: Its lacrimal and frontal branches pass through the lateral part of the fissure

The lacrimal and frontal branches of V1 enter the orbit through the lateral part of the superior orbital fissure, outside the tendinous ring.
IV enters with them. (Last's p. 567)
Its nasociliary branch enters the fibrous ring

The nasociliary branch slopes down to enter the fibrous (tendinous) ring.
It lies between the two divisions of III. (Last's p. 567)
All three branches are crossed laterally by the oculomotor nerve

The branches of V1 are crossed medially by III, not laterally.
III passes medial to them as it enters the ring. (Last's p. 567)
It gives off tentorial branches at the posterior end of the sinus

V1 gives off its tentorial branches at the anterior end of the cavernous sinus.
They then run back to supply the tentorium and falx. (Last's p. 567)
The superior ophthalmic vein enters the anterior end directly

The superior ophthalmic vein passes back through the superior orbital fissure directly into the front of the cavernous sinus.
That is the main route for facial infection to reach the sinus. (Last's p. 567)
The inferior ophthalmic veins drain partly to the pterygoid plexus

The inferior ophthalmic veins drain partly into the superior ophthalmic vein and partly through the inferior orbital fissure to the pterygoid plexus.
So the orbit connects with both the sinus and the infratemporal fossa. (Last's p. 567)
The superficial middle cerebral vein enters through the lateral wall

The superficial middle cerebral vein pierces the roof of the sinus near the emerging internal carotid artery, not the lateral wall.
Thrombosis can spread back along it to the hemisphere. (Last's p. 567)
Blood can only flow from front to back in the sinus

Blood can flow in either direction in the cavernous sinus, because the sinuses and their tributaries are valveless.
Flow direction depends on pressure. (Last's p. 567)

questions.s: Sinuses connected with the cavernous sinus:
o: The sphenoparietal sinus runs beneath the edge of the lesser wing

The sphenoparietal sinus runs beneath the edge of the lesser wing of the sphenoid and drains into the roof of the cavernous sinus.
It receives middle meningeal veins. (Last's p. 567)
The inferior petrosal sinus empties the bulk of its blood

The inferior petrosal sinus is the larger outflow and carries the bulk of the blood from the cavernous sinus.
It drains to the internal jugular vein. (Last's p. 567)
The superior petrosal sinus is larger than the inferior

The inferior petrosal sinus is larger than the superior petrosal sinus.
The superior one runs along the petrous ridge in the attached margin of the tentorium. (Last's p. 567)
The superior petrosal sinus drains into the jugular bulb

The superior petrosal sinus drains into the beginning of the sigmoid sinus, not the jugular bulb.
The inferior petrosal sinus drains to the internal jugular vein just below the skull. (Last's p. 567)
Leaves beneath the petroclinoid ligament

The inferior petrosal sinus leaves the back of the cavernous sinus beneath the petroclinoid ligament, with VI.
This is Dorello's canal. (Last's p. 567)
Enters the anterior compartment of the jugular foramen medial to IX

The inferior petrosal sinus enters the anterior compartment of the jugular foramen medial to IX and joins the internal jugular vein just below the skull.
It is the most medial structure in the foramen. (Last's p. 567)
Is the lowest tributary of the internal jugular vein

The inferior petrosal sinus is the first (highest) tributary of the internal jugular vein.
It joins just below the jugular foramen. (Last's p. 567)
Runs along the petro-occipital suture outside the dura

The inferior petrosal sinus runs along the petro-occipital suture between the two layers of dura.
All the main sinuses lie within the dura. (Last's p. 567)

questions.s: Other connections of the cavernous sinus:
o: An emissary vein usually passes through foramen ovale to the pterygoid plexus

An emissary vein usually passes through foramen ovale, linking the cavernous sinus with the pterygoid plexus.
This allows spread of infection from the infratemporal fossa. (Last's p. 567)
The foramen of Vesalius lies medial to foramen ovale

When present, the foramen of Vesalius lies medial to foramen ovale and carries an additional emissary vein.
It is a landmark in percutaneous trigeminal procedures. (Last's p. 567)
The intercavernous sinuses lie in the diaphragma sellae only

The intercavernous sinuses lie mainly between the dural layers lining the pituitary fossa, with a few in the diaphragma sellae.
They can bleed in trans-sphenoidal surgery. (Last's p. 567)
The petroclinoid ligament joins the petrous apex to the anterior clinoid

The petroclinoid ligament joins the petrous apex to the side of the dorsum sellae (posterior clinoid region), not to the anterior clinoid process.
VI and the inferior petrosal sinus pass beneath it. (Last's p. 567)
The danger area of the face lies above the level of the deep facial vein

The danger area of the face lies above the level of the deep facial vein, between the two routes linking facial skin to the cavernous sinus.
Infection here can spread to the sinus. (Last's p. 568)
It includes the upper lip, nose and medial cheek

The danger area includes the upper lip, nose and medial cheek, which drain via the angular–ophthalmic and deep facial–pterygoid routes to the sinus.
Squeezing boils here is dangerous. (Last's p. 568)
The ophthalmoplegia is usually fatal

Last's says the ophthalmoplegia of cavernous thrombosis is not itself dangerous. Retrograde thrombosis of the inferior petrosal sinus and medullary veins is what is usually fatal.
This was the pattern before antibiotics. (Last's p. 568)
The facial vein communicates directly with the sinus through foramen ovale

The facial vein connects with the sinus through the angular vein and superior ophthalmic vein, and through the deep facial vein and pterygoid plexus (with emissary veins).
There is no direct facial vein connection through foramen ovale. (Last's p. 568)
Usually involves the frontal branch of the middle meningeal

Fractures of the side of the skull usually tear the frontal (anterior) branch of the middle meningeal artery, causing extradural haemorrhage.
It runs in a bony tunnel at the pterion. (Last's p. 568)
May cause contralateral hemiparesis

The haematoma presses on the motor area and may cause contralateral hemiparesis.
A lucid interval often precedes deterioration. (Last's p. 568)
Causes pupil dilatation on the opposite side

The pupil dilates on the injured side, from compression of III by the herniating uncus.
The ipsilateral dilated pupil helps localise the clot. (Last's p. 568)
Compression of the anterior cerebral artery gives occipital ischaemia

Tentorial herniation compresses the posterior cerebral artery (not the anterior), which can cause occipital ischaemia.
The anterior cerebral can be compressed under the falx. (Last's p. 568)
Usually from a superior cerebral vein entering the superior sagittal sinus

Subdural haemorrhage usually comes from a bridging superior cerebral vein tearing as it enters the superior sagittal sinus.
The elderly and alcoholics, with brain atrophy, are most at risk. (Last's p. 568)
Symptoms develop more slowly than with extradural

Because the bleeding is venous, symptoms develop more slowly than with extradural haemorrhage, sometimes over weeks.
Chronic subdurals may present with confusion. (Last's p. 568)
Blood collects between arachnoid and pia

Subdural blood collects between the dura and arachnoid. Blood between arachnoid and pia is subarachnoid.
The name tells you the space. (Last's p. 568)
Symptoms are typically more severe than extradural

Last's says the symptoms of subdural haemorrhage are typically less severe and slower than those of extradural haemorrhage.
Arterial extradural bleeding builds pressure fast. (Last's p. 568)

questions.s: Contents of the anterior cranial fossa (Last's):
o: Up to 20 olfactory filaments pierce the meninges on each side

Up to 20 olfactory filaments on each side pierce the meninges over the cribriform plate.
Fractures here cause anosmia and CSF leaks. (Last's p. 568)
The anterior ethmoidal nerve enters near the back of the cribriform plate

The anterior ethmoidal nerve enters the fossa near the back of the cribriform plate and runs forward on it.
It then descends beside the crista galli. (Last's p. 568)
A patent vein through the foramen caecum is present in about 50%

A patent vein through the foramen caecum is present in only about 1 percent of people, not 50 percent.
Usually it is a blind pit plugged by the falx. (Last's p. 568)
The anterior ethmoidal nerve leaves through the foramen caecum

The anterior ethmoidal nerve leaves through a slit beside the front of the crista galli, not through the foramen caecum.
It then supplies the front of the nasal cavity. (Last's p. 568)

questions.s: Contents of the middle cranial fossa (Last's):
o: The median part contains the pituitary and optic chiasma

The median part of the middle cranial fossa contains the pituitary gland, the optic chiasma and the intercavernous sinuses.
This is the sellar region. (Last's p. 568-9)
The lateral parts contain the greater and lesser petrosal nerves

The greater and lesser petrosal nerves run in the lateral parts of the middle fossa on the anterior surface of the petrous bone.
They are hidden under the dura. (Last's p. 568-9)
The lateral parts contain the optic nerves

The optic nerves lie in the median part of the middle fossa, above the sella.
The lateral parts hold the temporal lobes. (Last's p. 568-9)
The median part contains the cavernous sinuses

The cavernous sinuses lie in the lateral parts of the middle fossa, on either side of the sella.
The median part holds the pituitary between them. (Last's p. 568-9)
The intercavernous sinuses lie below it

The intercavernous sinuses lie in the dura below (and around) the pituitary, linking the two cavernous sinuses.
They form a venous ring around the gland. (Last's p. 569)
Large sphenoid sinuses may extend back beneath the fossa

A small sphenoidal sinus lies in front of and below the pituitary fossa; a large one extends back beneath it.
The degree of pneumatisation affects the trans-sphenoidal approach. (Last's p. 569)
Pia and arachnoid around it are usually fused with the dura of the fossa

Last's says the pia and arachnoid around the pituitary lie against but are not fused with the dura of the fossa.
The subarachnoid space may extend down around the stalk. (Last's p. 569)
The stalk slopes downwards and backwards to the diaphragma

The pituitary stalk slopes downward and forward to the diaphragma sellae, not backward.
It runs from the tuber cinereum to the gland. (Last's p. 569)
The adenohypophysis arises from Rathke's pouch

The adenohypophysis arises from Rathke's pouch, an upgrowth of ectoderm from the roof of the primitive mouth.
Remnants can give rise to craniopharyngiomas. (Last's p. 569)
The neurohypophysis includes the median eminence

The neurohypophysis includes the median eminence, the infundibular stalk and the pars nervosa.
It is a downgrowth of the floor of the diencephalon. (Last's p. 569)
The pars intermedia belongs to the neurohypophysis

The pars intermedia belongs to the adenohypophysis (it comes from the back wall of Rathke's pouch).
It is small in humans. (Last's p. 569)
The pars tuberalis is a downgrowth of the third ventricle floor

The pars tuberalis is part of the adenohypophysis, wrapping around the stalk. It is not a downgrowth of the third ventricle floor.
The infundibulum is the downgrowth. (Last's p. 569)
The pars distalis is about 75% of the gland

The pars distalis (anterior lobe) makes up about 75 percent of the gland.
It secretes the trophic hormones, growth hormone and prolactin. (Last's p. 569)
Acidophils secrete growth hormone and prolactin

Acidophils (35 percent) secrete growth hormone and prolactin. Basophils (15 percent) secrete the trophic hormones.
Chromophobes make up the remaining 50 percent. (Last's p. 569)
Basophils make up 35% of pars distalis cells

Basophils make up about 15 percent of pars distalis cells. Acidophils make up 35 percent and chromophobes 50 percent.
The numbers 50, 35, 15 are worth remembering. (Last's p. 569)
The pars intermedia probably secretes ACTH

Last's says the pars intermedia probably secretes MSH (melanocyte-stimulating hormone), not ACTH.
ACTH comes from the basophils of the pars distalis. (Last's p. 569)
Contains about 100 000 unmyelinated axons

The pars nervosa contains about 100 000 unmyelinated axons from the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei.
Their hormones are stored in axon terminals. (Last's p. 569)
Oxytocin comes mainly from paraventricular cells

Oxytocin comes mainly from paraventricular cells. Vasopressin comes mainly from supraoptic cells.
Both nuclei produce some of each. (Last's p. 569)
Vasopressin comes mainly from paraventricular cells

Vasopressin comes mainly from supraoptic cells. Oxytocin comes mainly from paraventricular cells.
"Supraoptic = ADH". (Last's p. 569)
Pituicytes resemble oligodendrocytes

Pituicytes resemble astrocytes, not oligodendrocytes.
They are the glial cells of the posterior lobe. (Last's p. 569)
Hypophyseal arteries arise from ICA, ACA and PCA

The superior and inferior hypophyseal arteries arise from the internal carotid and the anterior and posterior cerebral arteries.
The superior arteries supply the median eminence and stalk. (Last's p. 569-70)
Portal vessels carry hypophysiotropic hormones to the anterior lobe

Releasing hormones from the median eminence reach the anterior lobe through the hypophyseal portal vessels.
So the anterior lobe receives mainly portal blood. (Last's p. 569-70)
Posterior lobe hormones reach it by portal vessels

Posterior lobe hormones are made in hypothalamic neurons and stored in the axons that made them; they do not arrive by portal vessels.
The portal system serves the anterior lobe. (Last's p. 569-70)
The transsphenoidal approach enters the nasal cavity proper

In the trans-sphenoidal approach the nasal cavity itself is not entered; the dissection is submucosal along the septum.
This reduces infection and bleeding. (Last's p. 569-70)
Curves immediately backwards on the roof of the sinus

After emerging through the roof of the cavernous sinus, the internal carotid curves immediately backward on the roof, then upward lateral to the chiasma.
This forms the upper limb of the siphon. (Last's p. 570)
Gives the ophthalmic artery immediately above the roof

The ophthalmic artery arises immediately above the roof of the cavernous sinus, below the optic nerve.
It enters the orbit through the optic canal. (Last's p. 570)
In the optic canal the artery lies above and medial to the nerve

In the optic canal the ophthalmic artery lies below and lateral to the nerve.
It later crosses above the nerve in the orbit. (Last's p. 570)
The carotid siphon is a U opening forwards

The carotid siphon is a U-shaped bend opening backward, not forward.
Its shape is seen on lateral angiograms. (Last's p. 570)

questions.s: The oculomotor nerve in the middle fossa (Last's):
o: Runs parallel to and just below the posterior communicating artery

III runs parallel to and just below the posterior communicating artery. Aneurysms of that artery may damage it.
A painful III palsy needs urgent imaging. (Last's p. 570)
Pupillary fibres lie on the outer part of the nerve

Pupillary fibres lie peripherally on the outer part of III, so external compression by an aneurysm dilates the pupil early.
They are supplied by the nerve sheath vessels. (Last's p. 570)
Diabetic infarction typically affects the pupillary fibres first

Diabetic infarction affects the core of the nerve and may spare the peripheral pupillary fibres.
A pupil-sparing III palsy suggests ischaemia rather than compression. (Last's p. 570)
Pupillary fibres lie ventral at the brainstem then lateral

Last's says the pupillary fibres lie first dorsally, then medially, then inferiorly along the nerve.
They are always superficial. (Last's p. 570)

questions.s: The trochlear nerve in the middle fossa:
o: Curls round the peduncle below the posterior cerebral artery

IV curls round the cerebral peduncle below the posterior cerebral artery and above the superior cerebellar artery.
III passes between the same two arteries more medially. (Last's p. 570)
Lies lateral to the oculomotor in the interpeduncular cistern

In the interpeduncular cistern IV lies lateral to III, between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries.
It is much thinner than III. (Last's p. 570)
Enters the middle fossa in front of the oculomotor nerve

IV enters the middle fossa just behind III, not in front of it.
Both pierce the roof of the cavernous sinus near the crossing of the tentorial margins. (Last's p. 570)
Runs above the free margin of the tentorium

IV runs just below the free margin of the tentorium, in the posterior fossa.
It is vulnerable when the tentorial edge is incised. (Last's p. 570)
The nerve leaves a groove about 5 mm wide on the petrous border

The trigeminal roots make a shallow groove about 5 mm wide on the upper border of the petrous bone near its apex.
This is the trigeminal notch. (Last's p. 570)
It passes beneath the superior petrosal sinus

The roots pass beneath the superior petrosal sinus into the mouth of the trigeminal cave.
The sinus runs along the petrous ridge. (Last's p. 570)
The greater petrosal nerve lies above the cave

The greater petrosal nerve lies beneath the trigeminal cave, not above it.
It runs towards foramen lacerum under the ganglion. (Last's p. 570)
The mouth of the cave opens forwards into the middle fossa

The mouth of the trigeminal cave opens backward into the posterior fossa, where the root enters.
The ganglion lies in the middle fossa. (Last's p. 570)

questions.s: Blood and nerve supply of the trigeminal ganglion:
o: The accessory meningeal artery brings appreciable blood

The accessory meningeal artery brings an appreciable blood supply to the trigeminal ganglion, running up along the mandibular division.
The ganglion also gets internal carotid and middle meningeal branches. (Last's p. 571)
The nervus spinosus supplies its epineurium

The nervus spinosus supplies the ganglion's epineurium and the nearby dura.
Nerves themselves have nerve supplies to their sheaths. (Last's p. 571)
Its nerve supply is from the tentorial nerve

The nerve supply of the trigeminal ganglion's sheath is from the nervus spinosus, not the tentorial nerve.
The tentorial nerve (V1) supplies the tentorium and falx. (Last's p. 571)
The mandibular division touches the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus

Last's says the mandibular division never contacts the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus.
It passes straight down to foramen ovale. (Last's p. 571)
The greater petrosal runs beneath the trigeminal ganglion

The greater petrosal nerve runs beneath the trigeminal ganglion, between the dural layers of the middle fossa floor.
It heads for foramen lacerum. (Last's p. 571)
The Vidian nerve enters the posterior end of the pterygoid canal

In the foramen lacerum the greater and deep petrosal nerves join as the Vidian nerve, which enters the posterior end of the pterygoid canal.
It runs forward to the pterygopalatine ganglion. (Last's p. 571)
The lesser petrosal comes from the facial nerve

The lesser petrosal nerve comes from the glossopharyngeal nerve (via its tympanic branch and plexus).
The greater petrosal comes from the facial nerve. (Last's p. 571)
The lesser petrosal nerve joins the pterygopalatine ganglion

The lesser petrosal nerve joins the otic ganglion. The greater petrosal goes to the pterygopalatine ganglion.
Lesser = parotid; greater = lacrimal. (Last's p. 571)

questions.s: The abducent nerve in the posterior fossa (Last's):
o: Emerges near the ventral midline at the pontomedullary junction

VI emerges close to the ventral midline at the junction of the pons and pyramid.
It runs upward on the clivus. (Last's p. 571)
Its long intracranial course makes it vulnerable to raised pressure

Its long intracranial course over the petrous apex makes VI vulnerable to raised pressure, so lateral rectus palsy can be a false localising sign.
It does not indicate a lesion near the nerve. (Last's p. 571)
It pierces the dura on the clivus below its origin

VI pierces the dura on the clivus some distance above its origin.
It then runs between the dural layers to the petrous apex. (Last's p. 571)
It enters the superior petrosal sinus

VI enters the inferior petrosal sinus at the petrous apex, then passes under the petroclinoid ligament.
The superior petrosal sinus runs along the petrous ridge, further up. (Last's p. 571)
The cochlea lies in front of the vestibule

In the petrous bone the cochlea lies in front of the vestibule, so the cochlear nerve lies in the front of the meatus.
The vestibular nerves lie behind. (Last's p. 572)
The facial nerve pierces the front of the upper part

The facial nerve enters the anterosuperior quadrant of the fundus of the meatus.
It goes into the facial canal. (Last's p. 572)
The vestibular nerve pierces the front of the lower part

The cochlear nerve pierces the front of the lower part of the fundus. The vestibular nerves pierce the posterior part.
"Seven up, Coke down" at the front. (Last's p. 572)
Inner dura is separate from the meatal endosteum

Last's says the inner layer of dura is fused with the meatal endosteum throughout.
The arachnoid and subarachnoid space extend into the meatus. (Last's p. 572)

questions.s: The posterior surface of the petrous bone:
o: The subarcuate fossa lodges the flocculus in the neonate

In the neonate the subarcuate fossa is as large as the internal meatus and lodges the flocculus of the cerebellum.
It shrinks to a small pit in the adult. (Last's p. 572)
The endolymphatic sac lies beneath the inner layer of dura

The endolymphatic sac hangs down from the vestibular aqueduct beneath the inner layer of dura on the posterior surface of the petrous bone.
It is involved in endolymph absorption. (Last's p. 572)
The subarcuate fossa lies medial to the internal meatus

The subarcuate fossa lies lateral to the internal acoustic meatus, below the arcuate eminence.
It transmits a small vein. (Last's p. 572)
The vestibular aqueduct opens medial to the internal meatus

The vestibular aqueduct opens further laterally on the posterior surface, not medial to the meatus.
The endolymphatic sac lies at its opening. (Last's p. 572)
It is divided by two dural septa that may ossify

Two fibrous dural septa divide the jugular foramen into three compartments, and they sometimes ossify.
Anterior: inferior petrosal sinus and IX; middle: X and XI; posterior: jugular bulb. (Last's p. 572)
IX and X and XI pass laterally behind the jugular tubercle

IX, X and XI pass laterally behind the jugular tubercle in that order, to reach the jugular foramen.
The tubercle is a landmark in far lateral approaches. (Last's p. 572)
The vagus lies lateral to the accessory nerve

The accessory nerve lies lateral to the vagus in the jugular foramen.
From medial to lateral: inferior petrosal sinus, IX, X, XI. (Last's p. 572)
The inferior petrosal sinus groove enters lateral to the cochlear canaliculus notch

The groove for the inferior petrosal sinus enters medial to the notch for the cochlear canaliculus.
The sinus is the most medial structure. (Last's p. 572)
The canal lies at the junction of basiocciput and jugular process

The hypoglossal canal lies at the old epiphyseal junction between the basiocciput and the jugular (lateral) part of the occipital bone, above the condyle.
It runs forward and laterally. (Last's p. 573)
Its two roots are separated by dura that occasionally ossifies

A dural flange separates the two roots of XII in the canal and occasionally ossifies to give a double canal.
The roots unite within the canal. (Last's p. 573)
The rootlets arise between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle

The hypoglossal rootlets arise between the pyramid and the olive.
IX, X and XI arise behind the olive. (Last's p. 573)
The roots unite before entering the canal

The two roots enter the canal separately and unite within it.
A flange of dura separates them at the entrance. (Last's p. 573)
Gives meningeal branches before piercing the spinal dura

The meningeal branches of the vertebral artery arise after it pierces the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane but before it pierces the dura.
They supply the posterior fossa dura. (Last's p. 573)
Runs in front of the denticulate ligament

Intradurally the vertebral artery runs in front of the denticulate ligament, between the rootlets of XII and C1.
It then curves forward around the medulla. (Last's p. 573)
Gives a single posterior spinal artery

The vertebral artery gives two small posterior spinal arteries, not one (although they often arise from PICA instead).
The anterior spinal artery is a single vessel formed from both sides. (Last's p. 573)
Joins its fellow at the upper border of the pons

The vertebral arteries join at the lower border of the pons to form the basilar artery.
The basilar divides at the upper border. (Last's p. 573)
Is usually curved to one side of the midline

The basilar artery usually curves to one side of the midline.
So it is not responsible for the median groove on the front of the pons. (Last's p. 573)
Gives the superior cerebellar arteries just before dividing

The basilar gives the superior cerebellar arteries just before ending as the two posterior cerebral arteries.
III emerges between these vessels. (Last's p. 573)
Produces the ventral median groove of the pons

Last's says the basilar artery is not responsible for the ventral median groove of the pons.
The groove is formed by the bulging corticospinal fibres on each side. (Last's p. 573)
Gives PICA

PICA arises from the vertebral artery, not the basilar.
AICA and the superior cerebellar arteries come from the basilar. (Last's p. 573)

questions.s: The superior view of the skull (Last's):
o: The coronal suture is straight for 3 cm or more lateral to bregma

The coronal suture is straight for 3 cm or more lateral to bregma. This marks the line of closure of the anterior fontanelle.
Beyond that it becomes tortuous. (Last's p. 643-4)
An emissary vein from the superior sagittal sinus passes through the parietal foramen

An emissary vein runs from the superior sagittal sinus through each parietal foramen to the scalp.
The foramina lie near the sagittal suture. (Last's p. 643-4)
The sagittal suture is tortuous for its anterior 3 cm

The anterior 3 cm of the sagittal suture are straight, then it becomes tortuous for about 5 cm.
The straight part again marks the anterior fontanelle. (Last's p. 643-4)
The parietal eminence lies at the posterior angle of the parietal bone

The parietal eminence lies at the centre of the parietal bone, the site where ossification began.
It is not at the posterior angle. (Last's p. 643-4)

questions.s: The posterior view of the skull (Last's):
o: Wormian bones may occur at the pterion

Wormian (sutural) bones may occur at the pterion as well as along the lambdoid suture.
They are small islands of bone within sutures. (Last's p. 644)
An interparietal bone results from failed fusion of cartilaginous and membranous occipital parts

An interparietal bone results from failure of fusion between the cartilaginous and membranous parts of the occipital bone. Last's says it is not an accessory bone.
It lies above the superior nuchal line. (Last's p. 644)
The external occipital protuberance lies about 2 cm below lambda

The external occipital protuberance lies about 6 cm below lambda, not 2 cm.
It is a palpable landmark in the midline. (Last's p. 644)
Trapezius attaches to the lateral two-thirds of the superior nuchal line

Trapezius attaches to the medial third of the superior nuchal line. Sternocleidomastoid attaches to the lateral two-thirds.
Splenius capitis lies deep to sternocleidomastoid. (Last's p. 644)
Splenius capitis inserts into the lateral third of the superior nuchal line

Splenius capitis inserts into the lateral third of the superior nuchal line, deep to sternocleidomastoid.
It extends and rotates the head. (Last's p. 644)
The highest nuchal line gives origin to occipitalis and the galea

The highest nuchal line gives origin to occipitalis and the galea aponeurotica.
It lies above the superior nuchal line. (Last's p. 644)
The superior nuchal line marks the internal attachment of the falx cerebri

The superior nuchal line marks the internal attachment of the tentorium, straddling the transverse sinus.
The falx cerebri attaches along the sagittal suture region above. (Last's p. 644)
The mastoid emissary vein connects the transverse sinus to the occipital vein

The mastoid emissary vein connects the sigmoid sinus with the posterior auricular vein.
It passes through the mastoid foramen. (Last's p. 644)

questions.s: The lateral view of the skull (Last's):
o: The coronal suture is tortuous above and straight below the inferior temporal line

The coronal suture is tortuous above the inferior temporal line and straight below it.
Under temporalis it runs straight down to the pterion. (Last's p. 644-5)
The pterion is an H-shaped area of four bones

The pterion is an H-shaped area where four bones meet: frontal, parietal, squamous temporal and greater wing of the sphenoid.
The middle meningeal artery lies deep to it. (Last's p. 644-5)
The squamous temporal overlaps the greater wing in the infratemporal fossa

In the infratemporal fossa the greater wing overlies the squamous temporal bone. In the temporal fossa the squamous temporal overlaps the greater wing.
The overlap reverses above and below the infratemporal crest. (Last's p. 644-5)
The asterion is where coronal and squamosal sutures meet

The asterion is where the parietal, temporal (mastoid part) and occipital bones meet.
The junction of the transverse and sigmoid sinuses lies deep to it. (Last's p. 644-5)
Temporalis fascia attaches to the superior line and the strip between the lines

The temporalis fascia attaches to the superior temporal line and the polished strip between the two temporal lines.
Temporalis muscle arises below the inferior line. (Last's p. 645)
The inferior temporal line runs into the suprameatal crest

The inferior temporal line curves back across the parietal bone and runs into the suprameatal crest.
The crest lies above the external acoustic meatus. (Last's p. 645)
The infratemporal crest is level with the lower border of the zygomatic arch

The infratemporal crest is level with the upper border of the zygomatic arch.
It separates the temporal from the infratemporal surface of the greater wing. (Last's p. 645)
The anterior wall of the temporal fossa is perforated by the zygomaticofacial nerve

The anterior wall of the temporal fossa is perforated by the zygomaticotemporal nerve.
The zygomaticofacial nerve emerges on the facial surface of the zygomatic bone. (Last's p. 645)
The temporal and zygomatic processes meet near the front of the arch

The zygomatic process of the temporal bone and the temporal process of the zygomatic bone meet at an oblique suture near the front of the arch.
Most of the arch is temporal bone. (Last's p. 646)
The deep head of masseter arises from the medial surface of the arch

The deep head of masseter arises from the deep (medial) surface of the zygomatic arch; the superficial head from its lower border.
The deep head inserts higher on the ramus. (Last's p. 646)
The temporomandibular ligament attaches to the medial surface of the articular tubercle

The temporomandibular (lateral) ligament attaches to the lateral surface of the articular tubercle, then runs down and back to the neck of the mandible.
It is the main ligament of the joint. (Last's p. 646)
The auriculotemporal nerve crosses the arch in front of the zygomatic branches of VII

The auriculotemporal nerve crosses the root of the arch just in front of the external acoustic meatus, behind the zygomatic branches of VII.
The superficial temporal vessels lie in front of it. (Last's p. 646)

questions.s: The lateral view of the maxilla and zygomatic bone:
o: Zygomaticus minor arises from the zygomaticomaxillary suture

Zygomaticus minor arises from the zygomaticomaxillary suture region; zygomaticus major arises from the zygomatic bone further laterally.
Both elevate the upper lip and angle of the mouth. (Last's p. 647)
The pyramidal process of the palatine is wedged between maxilla and lateral pterygoid plate

The pyramidal process of the palatine bone is wedged between the maxillary tuberosity and the lower part of the lateral pterygoid plate.
It gives origin to part of medial pterygoid. (Last's p. 647)
Buccinator arises from the alveolar margin of the maxilla

Buccinator arises from a line on the maxilla well above the alveolar bone, opposite the molars.
The same applies to its mandibular origin, below the alveolar margin. (Last's p. 647)
The pterygomaxillary ligament runs from the tuberosity to the lateral pterygoid plate

The pterygomaxillary ligament runs from the maxillary tuberosity to the tip of the pterygoid hamulus.
It is a landmark for the pterygomandibular region. (Last's p. 647)

questions.s: The anterior view of the skull (Last's):
o: The frontal bone occupies the upper third of the anterior view

In the anterior view the frontal bone makes up the upper third of the facial skeleton; the maxillae and mandible make the lower two-thirds.
Facial proportions change with age as the jaws grow. (Last's p. 647)
Supraorbital notch, infraorbital and mental foramina lie in a vertical line

The supraorbital notch, infraorbital foramen and mental foramen lie in one vertical line, useful for locating these nerves for blocks.
The line is about 2.5 cm from the midline. (Last's p. 647)
The nasal bones are notched by the infraorbital nerve

The nasal bones are notched (grooved) by the external nasal nerve, not the infraorbital nerve.
The external nasal nerve emerges between the nasal bone and the lateral cartilage. (Last's p. 647)
Levator anguli oris arises from the incisive fossa

Levator anguli oris arises from the canine fossa, below the infraorbital foramen.
The incisive fossa gives origin to the small incisive muscles. (Last's p. 647)

questions.s: The inferior view of the occipital bone (Last's):
o: Rectus capitis posterior minor attaches medially beside the foramen magnum

Rectus capitis posterior minor attaches to the occipital bone medially, beside the foramen magnum; the major attaches laterally to it.
Both lie below the inferior nuchal line. (Last's p. 648)
Semispinalis capitis attaches between the nuchal lines medially

Semispinalis capitis attaches between the superior and inferior nuchal lines medially; superior oblique attaches laterally.
These form the bulk of the back of the neck. (Last's p. 648)
Two-thirds of the foramen magnum lies in front of the mastoid line

One-third of the foramen magnum lies in front of the line joining the mastoid processes and two-thirds behind. The condyles have the reverse proportions.
This helps orient the skull base. (Last's p. 648)
The mastoid-pterygoid tubercle line slants at 30 degrees

Last's says the line from mastoid process to pterygoid tubercle slants at 45 degrees.
Many skull base foramina lie along it. (Last's p. 648)

questions.s: The 45 degree line on the skull base:
o: It is divided into thirds by the styloid process and sphenoid spine

The base of the styloid process and the sphenoid spine divide the mastoid–pterygoid tubercle line into thirds, locating the stylomastoid foramen and foramen spinosum.
A useful way to find foramina on a dry skull. (Last's p. 648)
Foramen ovale lies anteromedial to foramen spinosum

Foramen ovale lies in front of and medial to foramen spinosum on the 45 degree line.
V3 passes through it. (Last's p. 648)
The scaphoid fossa lies medial to the pterygoid tubercle

The scaphoid fossa lies lateral to the pterygoid tubercle, at the top of the medial pterygoid plate.
Tensor palati arises from it. (Last's p. 648)
The pharyngeal tubercle lies halfway between foramen magnum and vomer

The pharyngeal tubercle lies one-third of the way from the foramen magnum to the vomer, not halfway.
It gives attachment to the pharyngeal raphe. (Last's p. 648)
Its long diameter is anteroposterior

The foramen magnum is oval, longest from front to back.
The medulla and spinal cord pass through it. (Last's p. 648)
Its transverse diameter is less than a third of the bimastoid distance

Its transverse diameter is a little less than one-third of the distance between the mastoid processes.
A small foramen magnum (as in achondroplasia) can compress the cord. (Last's p. 648)
The tectorial membrane lies in front of the cruciform ligament

The tectorial membrane is adherent to the dura, behind the cruciform ligament.
From front to back: apical ligament, cruciform ligament, tectorial membrane, dura. (Last's p. 648)
Meningeal arteries lie inside the fibrous dura here

At the foramen magnum the meningeal arteries lie outside the fibrous dura.
They enter from the vertebral arteries before the dura is pierced. (Last's p. 648)
The alar ligaments attach medial to the anterior pole of each condyle

Each alar ligament attaches to a triangular area medial to the anterior pole of the occipital condyle.
The alar ligaments limit rotation of the head on the atlas. (Last's p. 649)
The posterior atlanto-occipital membrane attaches to more than half the margin

The posterior atlanto-occipital membrane attaches along the posterior margin of the foramen magnum, more than half its circumference.
The vertebral artery pierces it. (Last's p. 649)
Squamous and jugular parts fuse at the sixth year

The squamous and jugular parts of the occipital bone fuse at about the second year. The jugular parts fuse with the basiocciput at the sixth year.
So "sixth year" belongs to the basiocciput junction. (Last's p. 649)
The apical ligament lies behind the tectorial membrane

The apical ligament lies in front of the tectorial membrane, running from the dens to the anterior margin of the foramen magnum.
The tectorial membrane is the most posterior ligament. (Last's p. 649)
They permit nodding and some abduction but no rotation

The occipital condyles are oval, and the atlanto-occipital joint allows nodding and some lateral flexion, but no rotation.
Rotation occurs at the atlanto-axial joints. (Last's p. 649)
Incomplete fusion may give two articular surfaces

The condyle develops from two parts, so incomplete fusion can leave two separate articular facets.
A normal variant. (Last's p. 649)
They are covered with fibrocartilage

The occipital condyles are covered with hyaline cartilage, like most synovial joint surfaces.
Fibrocartilage covers the TMJ and sternoclavicular joint surfaces. (Last's p. 649)
The condylar canal transmits an emissary to the pterygoid plexus

The condylar canal transmits an emissary vein to the suboccipital venous plexus, not the pterygoid plexus.
It connects with the sigmoid sinus. (Last's p. 649)
Rectus capitis lateralis attaches to the jugular process

Rectus capitis lateralis inserts into the jugular process behind the jugular foramen.
It is a landmark for the far lateral approach. (Last's p. 649)
The occipital artery grooves the occipitomastoid suture

The occipital artery grooves the occipitomastoid suture, medial to the mastoid notch.
The posterior belly of digastric arises from the notch. (Last's p. 649)
Rectus capitis anterior inserts in front of longus capitis

Rectus capitis anterior inserts behind longus capitis, just in front of the condyle.
Longus capitis inserts further forward on the basiocciput. (Last's p. 649)
The basiocciput fuses with the basisphenoid 5 cm in front of the foramen magnum

The basiocciput fuses with the basisphenoid about 2.5 cm in front of the foramen magnum, at the spheno-occipital synchondrosis.
5 cm is the trap. (Last's p. 649)
Its base lies one-third of the way from mastoid tip to pterygoid tubercle

The base of the styloid process lies one-third of the way along the line from the mastoid tip to the pterygoid tubercle.
The stylomastoid foramen lies just behind it. (Last's p. 649-50)
Stylopharyngeus arises high up medially

Stylopharyngeus arises high on the medial side of the styloid process; stylohyoid high behind; styloglossus low in front.
Each arises in the direction of its target. (Last's p. 649-50)
Styloglossus arises high up posteriorly

Styloglossus arises low down in front of the styloid process. Stylohyoid arises high up behind.
Styloglossus runs forward into the tongue. (Last's p. 649-50)
The stylomastoid foramen lies in front of its base

The stylomastoid foramen lies behind the base of the styloid process.
VII emerges through it. (Last's p. 649-50)

questions.s: The petrous apex and foramen lacerum (Last's):
o: No suture forms between the petrous apex and greater wing

The petrous apex lodges between the basiocciput and the greater wing without forming sutures, often leaving a slit (the foramen lacerum region).
These are cartilaginous joints. (Last's p. 650)
Levator palati arises from the petrous apex

Levator palati arises from the petrous apex (and the cartilaginous auditory tube).
It elevates the soft palate. (Last's p. 650)
The greater petrosal nerve passes through the foramen lacerum to the exterior

Nothing major passes through the foramen lacerum to the exterior. The greater petrosal nerve runs above its fibrous floor into the pterygoid canal.
Only minute emissary veins traverse it. (Last's p. 650)
The auditory tube runs parallel to the skull base

The auditory tube angles down at about 20 degrees, not parallel to the skull base.
In infants it is more horizontal, which favours middle ear infection. (Last's p. 650)
Its vaginal process is indented by the styloid

The part of the tympanic plate indented by the styloid process is the vaginal process (sheath of the styloid).
It wraps around the styloid base. (Last's p. 650)
The stylomandibular ligament runs from the vaginal process to the mandibular angle

The stylomandibular ligament, a thickening of parotid fascia, runs from the vaginal process (and styloid) to the angle of the mandible.
It separates the parotid from the submandibular gland. (Last's p. 650)
The suprameatal triangle overlies the antrum about 5 mm deep

The suprameatal triangle overlies the mastoid antrum about 15 mm deep in the adult, not 5 mm.
In infants the antrum is more superficial. (Last's p. 650)
The tympanic part is C-shaped and open below

The tympanic part of the temporal bone is C-shaped and open above.
It forms the floor and sides of the external acoustic meatus. (Last's p. 650)
The tegmen tympani divides its medial end

A flange of the tegmen tympani divides the medial end of the squamotympanic fissure into the petrosquamous (in front) and petrotympanic (behind) fissures.
The flange reaches the surface between them. (Last's p. 651)
The chorda tympani emerges in the petrotympanic fissure

The chorda tympani emerges through the petrotympanic fissure.
It then joins the lingual nerve. (Last's p. 651)
The petrosquamous fissure lies behind the tegmen flange

The petrosquamous fissure lies in front of the tegmen flange, and the petrotympanic fissure behind it.
The chorda uses the posterior (petrotympanic) one. (Last's p. 651)
The tegmen flange forms the medial boundary of the bony auditory tube

The tegmen flange forms the lateral boundary of the bony part of the auditory tube.
The tube runs medially from the middle ear. (Last's p. 651)

questions.s: The greater wing on the skull base (Last's):
o: The upper head of lateral pterygoid arises from its infratemporal surface

The infratemporal surface of the greater wing (with the squamous temporal bone) gives origin to the upper head of lateral pterygoid.
The lower head arises from the lateral pterygoid plate. (Last's p. 651)
The sphenomandibular ligament attaches to the tip of the spine

The sphenomandibular ligament runs from the tip of the sphenoid spine to the lingula of the mandible.
It is a remnant of Meckel's cartilage. (Last's p. 651)
The petrosal foramen lies in front of foramen ovale

The petrosal foramen, when present, lies behind foramen ovale.
It transmits the lesser petrosal nerve. (Last's p. 651)
Tensor palati arises lateral to the spine of the sphenoid

Tensor palati arises from the area between the scaphoid fossa and the spine of the sphenoid (and the auditory tube).
It hooks around the hamulus. (Last's p. 651)
The medial plate forms the posterior boundary of the nose

The medial pterygoid plate forms the posterior boundary of the nasal cavity at the choanae.
The nasopharynx lies behind it. (Last's p. 652)
The pterygomandibular raphe attaches to the hamulus

The pterygomandibular raphe runs from the hamulus of the medial pterygoid plate to the mandible behind the third molar.
Buccinator and the superior constrictor attach to it. (Last's p. 652)
The pterygoid canal opening lies in line with the lateral pterygoid plate

The opening of the pterygoid canal lies in line with the medial pterygoid plate.
It opens on the front of the foramen lacerum. (Last's p. 652)
The lower head of lateral pterygoid arises from the medial surface of the lateral plate

The lower head of lateral pterygoid arises from the whole lateral surface of the lateral plate. Medial pterygoid arises from its medial surface.
Each pterygoid is named for its position, not its origin surface. (Last's p. 652)
The vomerovaginal canal carries a pharyngeal branch of the sphenopalatine artery

The vomerovaginal canal carries a tiny pharyngeal branch of the sphenopalatine artery.
It lies between the vomer and the vaginal process of the sphenoid. (Last's p. 652)
The palatovaginal canal carries the pharyngeal nerve of the pterygopalatine ganglion

The palatovaginal canal carries the pharyngeal nerve of the pterygopalatine ganglion, with the pharyngeal artery, to the nasopharynx.
It runs backward from the fossa. (Last's p. 652)
The palatovaginal canal opens into the infratemporal fossa

The palatovaginal canal opens into the pterygopalatine fossa, not the infratemporal fossa.
Its other end opens into the nasal vault. (Last's p. 652)
The palatovaginal canal opens at the very back of the nasal vault

Last's says the palatovaginal canal opens about half a centimetre in front of the posterior limit of the nasal vault.
A small detail often used as a trap. (Last's p. 652)
Sutures ossify from within out, starting about age 40

Skull sutures close (ossify) from the inner table outward, beginning at about 40 years.
Their closure is unreliable for estimating age. (Last's p. 653)
The middle fossa floor is level with the upper border of the zygomatic arch

The floor of the middle cranial fossa is level with the upper border of the zygomatic arch. The anterior fossa is level with the upper orbital margin.
These surface levels guide burr holes. (Last's p. 653)
The anterior fossa floor is level with the lower orbital margin

The anterior fossa floor is level with the upper margin of the orbit, not the lower.
The orbit lies below the anterior fossa. (Last's p. 653)
The optic canals lie in the anterior cranial fossa

The optic canals lie in the middle cranial fossa.
The boundary is the front edge of the prechiasmatic groove. (Last's p. 653)
The olfactory bulb lies at the posterolateral angle of the cribriform plate

The olfactory bulb lies in a shallow fossa at the posterolateral angle of the cribriform plate.
The tract runs back from it. (Last's p. 653)
The anterior ethmoidal nerve enters the nose via the nasal slit

The anterior ethmoidal nerve passes into the roof of the nose through the slit beside the crista galli (the "nasal slit").
It then supplies the front of the nasal cavity. (Last's p. 653)
The foramen caecum perforates the frontal bone in most skulls

The foramen caecum perforates the frontal bone in only about 1 percent of skulls.
Usually it is a blind pit. (Last's p. 653)
The trochlear fovea lies above the floor of the frontal sinus

The trochlear fovea, for the pulley of superior oblique, lies below the floor of the frontal sinus.
It is on the orbital surface near the medial angle. (Last's p. 653)
The middle clinoid lies at the lateral end of the tuberculum sellae

The middle clinoid process is a small elevation at the lateral end of the tuberculum sellae, medial to the carotid groove.
It may join the anterior clinoid, forming a caroticoclinoid foramen. (Last's p. 653-4)
The ICA grooves the medial edge of the anterior clinoid

As it leaves the cavernous sinus, the internal carotid artery grooves the medial edge of the anterior clinoid process.
Anterior clinoidectomy exposes this segment. (Last's p. 653-4)
The optic chiasma lies directly over the prechiasmatic groove

The optic chiasma lies at a higher level, well behind the prechiasmatic groove, not directly over it.
The groove is misnamed in that sense. (Last's p. 653-4)
The lingula lies on the medial side of the carotid groove

The lingula of the sphenoid is the lateral ridge of the carotid groove, not the medial side.
It lies beside the foramen lacerum. (Last's p. 653-4)
The petroclinoid ligament reaches halfway up the dorsum sellae

The petroclinoid ligament runs from the petrous apex to about halfway up the side of the dorsum sellae; VI passes beneath it.
This is Dorello's canal. (Last's p. 654)
The arcuate eminence overlies the anterior semicircular canal

The arcuate eminence on the upper surface of the petrous bone is raised by the anterior (superior) semicircular canal. It is a landmark in middle fossa approaches.
The canal lies just beneath. (Last's p. 654)
The lesser petrosal groove lies posteromedial to the greater petrosal groove

The groove for the lesser petrosal nerve lies anterolateral to the greater petrosal groove, not posteromedial.
Both run forward and medially. (Last's p. 654)
The trigeminal motor root lies superficial to the sensory root in its groove

In its groove on the petrous apex, the trigeminal motor root lies deep to the sensory root.
The sensory root is the larger and more superficial. (Last's p. 654)
The accessory meningeal artery passes through foramen ovale
