The accessory meningeal artery passes up through foramen ovale and gives an appreciable supply to the trigeminal ganglion.
It comes from the maxillary or middle meningeal artery. (Last's p. 654)
The nervus spinosus commonly accompanies the accessory meningeal artery through foramen ovale

Last's says the nervus spinosus often enters through foramen ovale with the accessory meningeal artery, rather than through foramen spinosum.
Classically it is named after foramen spinosum. (Last's p. 654)
Foramen rotundum opens into the infratemporal fossa

Foramen rotundum opens into the pterygopalatine fossa, not the infratemporal fossa.
Foramen ovale opens into the infratemporal fossa. (Last's p. 654)
Foramen ovale lies posterolateral to foramen spinosum

Foramen ovale lies anteromedial to foramen spinosum.
Spinosum is posterolateral. (Last's p. 654)
It is closed by dura lateral to the line of foramen rotundum

Lateral to the line of foramen rotundum, the superior orbital fissure is closed by dura passing between the greater and lesser wings.
So only the medial part of the fissure is open. (Last's p. 654-5)
Its medial end transmits the front of the cavernous sinus and its nerves

The open medial end of the fissure receives the front of the cavernous sinus and transmits its nerves into the orbit.
These are III, IV, V1 and VI, with the ophthalmic veins. (Last's p. 654-5)
The sphenoparietal sinus runs above the lesser wing

The sphenoparietal sinus runs below the margin of the lesser wing, not above it.
It drains into the cavernous sinus. (Last's p. 654-5)
The nervus spinosus passes to the mastoid through the greater wing

The nervus spinosus passes to the mastoid air cells through the junction of the squamous and petrous parts of the temporal bone, not through the greater wing.
It is the nerve of the first pharyngeal pouch. (Last's p. 654-5)
The larger jugular foramen usually receives the superior sagittal blood

The larger jugular foramen, more commonly the right, usually receives the blood of the superior sagittal sinus.
The left usually receives the straight sinus. (Last's p. 655)
The jugular tubercle marks fusion of basiocciput and lateral parts

The jugular tubercle marks the line of fusion of the basiocciput with the lateral (jugular) parts of the occipital bone, above the hypoglossal canal.
It is a landmark in far lateral approaches. (Last's p. 655)
The narrower transverse groove receives the superior sagittal sinus

The narrower transverse groove receives the straight sinus. The wider one receives the superior sagittal sinus.
Usually the right is wider. (Last's p. 655)
The hypoglossal canal lies below the occipital condyle

The hypoglossal canal lies between the jugular tubercle (above) and the occipital condyle (below).
It runs above the condyle. (Last's p. 655)
Runs from foramen magnum to dorsum sellae

The clivus is the sloping groove from the foramen magnum up to the dorsum sellae.
It is formed by the basiocciput and basisphenoid. (Last's p. 655)
Its upper broader part lodges the pons

Below, the medulla lies between the jugular tubercles; above, the broader clivus lodges the pons.
The basilar artery lies on it. (Last's p. 655)
The inferior petrosal groove lies between basiocciput and sphenoid

The groove for the inferior petrosal sinus lies between the basiocciput and the petrous temporal bone, along the petro-occipital fissure.
Not between the basiocciput and sphenoid. (Last's p. 655)
The falx cerebelli attaches to the internal occipital protuberance only

The falx cerebelli attaches along the internal occipital crest, not just to the protuberance.
It extends down towards the foramen magnum. (Last's p. 655)
The frontal bone ossifies wholly in membrane

The frontal bone ossifies wholly in membrane, from two centres above the orbital margins.
It is part of the vault. (Last's p. 656-7)
The pterygoid canal lies lower and more medial than foramen rotundum

The pterygoid canal, almost as large as foramen rotundum, lies lower and more medial, in line with the medial pterygoid plate.
Both open into the pterygopalatine fossa. (Last's p. 656-7)
The metopic suture normally unites at birth

The metopic suture normally unites in the second year, not at birth.
It sometimes persists into adult life. (Last's p. 656-7)
The sphenoidal septum is usually central

Last's says the septum between the sphenoidal sinuses is always deviated, not central.
Surgeons must not assume it marks the midline. (Last's p. 656-7)
The body and lesser wing ossify in cartilage

The body and lesser wings of the sphenoid, and the base of the greater wings, ossify in cartilage.
They are part of the chondrocranium. (Last's p. 657)
The pterygoid plates ossify in membrane

The rest of the greater wings and the pterygoid plates ossify in membrane.
So the sphenoid is a mixed bone. (Last's p. 657)
The whole greater wing ossifies in cartilage

Only the base of the greater wing ossifies in cartilage; the rest is membrane bone.
The wing extends into the vault. (Last's p. 657)
The optic canal perforates the greater wing

The optic canal perforates the base of the lesser wing, not the greater wing.
The superior orbital fissure separates the two wings. (Last's p. 657)
The ICA bends through a right angle in the carotid canal

The internal carotid artery enters the carotid canal and turns forward through a right angle in the petrous bone.
It then runs horizontally to the petrous apex. (Last's p. 657)
The upper semicanal is for tensor tympani

A thin bony septum divides the musculotubular canal: tensor tympani lies in the upper semicanal, the bony auditory tube in the lower.
The canal opens into the front of the middle ear. (Last's p. 657)
The lower semicanal is for tensor tympani

The lower semicanal is the bony part of the auditory tube. Tensor tympani lies in the upper one.
The muscle is above, the tube below. (Last's p. 657)
The septum divides it vertically

The septum divides the canal horizontally into upper and lower parts.
Not vertically. (Last's p. 657)

questions.s: Ossification of the temporal and occipital bones (Last's):
o: The styloid process belongs to the second arch

The styloid process is second-arch cartilage (Reichert's), not part of the skull proper, and begins ossifying around birth.
It may elongate with ossification of the stylohyoid ligament (Eagle's syndrome). (Last's p. 658)
The squamous and tympanic parts ossify at the eighth week

The squamous and tympanic parts of the temporal bone are membrane bone, ossifying at the eighth embryonic week.
The petrous part ossifies in cartilage later. (Last's p. 658)
The occipital centres appear at the end of the fourth month

The occipital ossification centres appear at the end of the second month, not the fourth.
The occipital is one of the first skull bones to ossify. (Last's p. 658)
The jugular parts fuse with the basiocciput at the second year

The jugular parts fuse with the basiocciput at the sixth year. The squamous and jugular parts fuse at about the second year.
Two different fusion times. (Last's p. 658)
Its inferior border is bevelled and overlapped by the squamous temporal

The lower border of the parietal bone is bevelled where the squamous temporal bone overlaps it.
This squamous suture is a scale-like overlap. (Last's p. 658)
Its ossification centre appears at the future parietal eminence

The parietal bone ossifies in membrane from one centre at the site of the future parietal eminence.
The eminence remains the most prominent point. (Last's p. 658)
It ossifies in cartilage

The parietal bone ossifies in membrane, before the eighth week, not in cartilage.
It is a vault bone. (Last's p. 658)
Its anteroinferior angle articulates with the temporal bone

The anteroinferior angle of the parietal bone articulates with the greater wing of the sphenoid, at the pterion.
The temporal bone meets the inferior border. (Last's p. 658)
Its lateral labyrinth wall is the orbital plate (lamina papyracea)

The orbital plate (lamina papyracea) is the paper-thin lateral wall of the ethmoid labyrinth, forming much of the medial wall of the orbit.
Ethmoiditis easily spreads through it. (Last's p. 658)
The labyrinth ossifies in cartilage at the fifth month

The ethmoid labyrinth ossifies in cartilage at the fifth month, complete before birth.
The air cells are small at birth. (Last's p. 658)
The cribriform plate ossifies before birth

The cribriform plate ossifies at about one year, with the crista galli and perpendicular plate, not before birth.
So the midline ethmoid is cartilaginous at birth. (Last's p. 658)
The crista galli projects down from the cribriform plate

The crista galli projects up from the cribriform plate into the cranial cavity. The perpendicular plate projects down into the nasal septum.
The falx attaches to the crista. (Last's p. 658)

questions.s: Structures passing through foramen ovale include:
o: The mandibular nerve

The mandibular nerve passes through foramen ovale; its sensory and motor roots unite there.
It then divides in the infratemporal fossa. (Last's p. 658)
The accessory meningeal artery

The accessory meningeal artery passes up through foramen ovale to supply the trigeminal ganglion and dura.
It is part of the "OVALE" contents. (Last's p. 658)
An emissary vein from the cavernous sinus

An emissary vein links the cavernous sinus and pterygoid plexus through foramen ovale.
Mnemonic OVALE: Otic ganglion nearby, V3, Accessory meningeal, Lesser petrosal, Emissary vein. (Last's p. 658)
The middle meningeal artery

The middle meningeal artery passes through foramen spinosum.
Spinosum lies just posterolateral to ovale. (Last's p. 658)
The spinal roots of the accessory nerves pass through it

The spinal roots of XI ascend through the foramen magnum to join the cranial roots.
They then leave through the jugular foramen. (Last's p. 658)
The vertebral arteries pass through it

The vertebral arteries enter the skull through the foramen magnum, with the medulla and the spinal vessels.
They lie anterolateral to the medulla. (Last's p. 658)
The hypoglossal nerves pass through it

The hypoglossal nerves leave through the hypoglossal canals, not the foramen magnum.
The canals lie above the condyles. (Last's p. 658)
The brain weighs about 500 g in CSF

The brain weighs about 1500 g out of CSF but only about 50 g in CSF, because of buoyancy.
500 g is the trap. (Last's p. 658)
Foramen rotundum opens into it

Foramen rotundum opens forward into the upper part of the pterygopalatine fossa, carrying V2.
The pterygoid canal opens below and medial to it. (Last's p. 658)
The pterygoid process forms its posterior wall

The front of the pterygoid process forms the posterior wall of the pterygopalatine fossa, containing foramen rotundum and the pterygoid canal.
The maxilla forms the anterior wall. (Last's p. 658)
Its medial wall is the lateral pterygoid plate

The medial wall of the pterygopalatine fossa is the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone, with the sphenopalatine foramen.
The lateral pterygoid plate lies outside the fossa. (Last's p. 658)
It communicates laterally through the inferior orbital fissure

Laterally the fossa communicates through the pterygomaxillary fissure with the infratemporal fossa. The inferior orbital fissure is its superior communication, with the orbit.
The maxillary artery enters through the pterygomaxillary fissure. (Last's p. 658)
It is the lower end of the medial pterygoid plate

The pterygoid hamulus is the hooked lower end of the medial pterygoid plate.
It can be felt in the mouth behind the upper third molar. (Last's p. 658)
Tensor palati turns around it

The tendon of tensor palati hooks round the hamulus to become the palatine aponeurosis.
The hamulus acts as a pulley. (Last's p. 658)
It gives attachment to the stylomandibular ligament

The hamulus gives attachment to the pterygomaxillary ligament and the pterygomandibular raphe, not the stylomandibular ligament.
The stylomandibular ligament runs from the styloid to the angle of the mandible. (Last's p. 658)
The pterygomandibular raphe attaches to the lateral plate

The pterygomandibular raphe attaches to the hamulus of the medial plate, not to the lateral plate.
It runs down to the mandible behind the third molar. (Last's p. 658)
